title: What does a management consulting firm actually do?
description: A plain-English explanation of what consulting firms sell, who hires them, what a project looks like and why companies pay for outside advice.
hook: A management consulting firm sells the time and judgement of a small team that helps an organisation answer a hard question or make a change it cannot easily make alone. Clients pay for focus, outside experience and an independent view, usually for a project lasting weeks or months. Here is what firms sell, who buys it, how a project runs and why your case interview is a miniature of the job.

The short answer

A client hires a team of consultants for a set period to answer a specific question ("Should we enter Brazil?") or deliver a specific change ("Cut procurement costs by 10% this year"). The firm is paid for that team's time and expertise, usually as a fee agreed for the project. The client keeps the decision. The consultants' job is to make the decision better informed, faster and easier for the leadership team to agree on, and often to help carry it out.

Why a company pays for outside help

Large companies employ plenty of clever people, so the question is fair. There are four common reasons.

  • Focus. Executives are busy running the business. A consulting team can spend eight weeks on one problem, full time, without a day job pulling it away.
  • Pattern recognition. A firm may have seen the same problem at dozens of other companies and industries, so it knows which analyses matter and which solutions tend to work.
  • Independence. An outside team can say things insiders find awkward, test a pet project without politics, and help a divided leadership team agree.
  • Specialist skills. Pricing, supply chains, mergers, technology and advanced analytics need expertise a company may not want to keep in-house all year.

Most projects involve more than one. A board weighing an acquisition wants independence and deal experience; a hospital cutting waiting times wants operations specialists and spare capacity.

Who the clients are and what they ask

Clients include large companies in every industry, private equity funds, governments and public bodies, and non-profits. The person who hires the team is usually a senior executive, such as a chief executive, a division head or a fund partner, and the consultants work day to day with that executive's own staff.

The questions are almost exactly the ones you practise in case interviews:

  • Why are our profits falling, and what do we do about it?
  • Should we enter this market, and how?
  • Should we buy this company, and what is it worth to us?
  • How do we take 15% out of our cost base without hurting service?
  • How do we make this hospital, airport or government service run better?

That overlap is deliberate. Firms design case interviews to look like the work, so that the interview tests the skills the job needs. If the categories are new to you, our guide to case types maps each one.

How a project runs

Every firm and project differs, but most follow a similar arc.

1. Scoping

The team and the client agree the exact question, the deadline, what is in and out of scope, and what a good outcome looks like. A vague brief ("help us grow") becomes a precise one ("identify $200M of new revenue within three years from our existing customers").

2. Hypotheses and a work plan

The team writes down early guesses at the answer and plans the analysis needed to prove or disprove each one. This is hypothesis-driven thinking: it stops a team from boiling the ocean.

3. Analysis

The bulk of the time. The team gathers data, interviews managers, customers and experts, builds models and visits sites, revising the hypotheses as evidence arrives.

4. Synthesis

Findings become a clear story and recommendation, usually a slide document built on the pyramid principle: answer first, then the supporting arguments, then the evidence.

5. Decision and, often, implementation

The team presents to leadership or a steering committee. Many projects then continue into helping the client make the change happen: planning the roll-out, running pilots, tracking results.

A worked example: 40 smaller shops

Here is a simplified version of the kind of question a team might tackle. The numbers are illustrative.

A retailer with 200 large stores is considering opening 40 smaller convenience-format shops. Management's own estimate is that each shop costs $1.5M to open and will take $3.0M a year in sales at a 12% operating margin.

  • Profit per shop before side effects: $3.0M × 12% = $360k a year.
  • Cannibalisation. Customer research suggests each new shop will pull about $400k of sales away from nearby large stores, which earn 25% on those sales. Lost profit = $400k × 25% = $100k.
  • Net profit per shop: $360k − $100k = $260k a year.
  • All 40 shops: 40 × $260k = $10.4M a year, for an investment of 40 × $1.5M = $60M.
  • Payback: $60M ÷ $10.4M ≈ 5.8 years.

If the board wants its money back within five years, the plan as a whole fails. But the team does not stop at the average. Site-by-site modelling might show that 15 locations, in dense areas far from existing stores, earn about $450k each. Those 15 cost 15 × $1.5M = $22.5M and earn 15 × $450k = $6.75M a year: a payback of about 3.3 years.

The recommendation becomes: open the best 15 sites first, measure real performance against the model for a year, and decide on the rest with evidence. That is what the client buys. Not a deck for its own sake, but a better decision, the numbers behind it and a plan to act. Cannibalisation and payback are exactly the ideas you will use in interviews.

Strategy is only part of the business

Strategy work ("what should we do?") is the best-known part of consulting, but a large share of the industry is operations, technology and implementation work ("how do we do it, and do it well?"). Those projects tend to be longer, with bigger teams working inside the client's organisation. The types of consulting explains the differences, and the map of top firms shows who does what.

What this means for your case interview

A case interview asks you to run a 30-minute version of the project above: define the question, plan the analysis, work the numbers and land a recommendation a busy executive could act on. Interviewers are asking themselves whether they could put you in front of a client.

Compare two endings to the retailer case.

"So there are lots of factors. The payback is about six years, and there is cannibalisation, and it depends on the sites."
"I'd recommend opening 15 of the 40 shops. Across all 40, payback is nearly six years, above the five-year target, but the best 15 pay back in about three. The main risk is that cannibalisation is higher than the research suggests, so I'd pilot and track sales at nearby stores before committing the other $37.5M."

The second answer gives a decision, the numbers behind it and the main uncertainty. After each practice case, ask: if the chief executive had one minute, could they act on what I said?

Common misconceptions

  • "Consultants just tell clients what they already know." Sometimes the answer confirms a hunch, but the value is in the evidence and the agreement it creates. A board commits $60M on a quantified case, not an opinion.
  • "It is all slides." Slides carry the findings. The work behind them is data, interviews, models and judgement.
  • "Consultants make the decision." They recommend. The client decides and owns the result.

Practice

1. A friend asks, "Why would a bank pay a consulting firm when it has its own strategy team?" Answer in three sentences.

Show the answer

Its strategy team is small and busy with day-to-day priorities, so an outside team can add focused capacity for a few months. A consulting firm may have solved the same problem at other banks and in other industries, so it knows what tends to work. And an independent view can help a divided leadership team agree, or test an idea without internal politics.

2. In the retailer example, what would the payback on all 40 shops be if cannibalisation were zero?

Show the answer

Profit per shop would be $360k, so 40 shops earn $14.4M a year on a $60M investment. Payback = $60M ÷ $14.4M ≈ 4.2 years, which would clear a five-year target. Cannibalisation is the difference between yes and no, which is why the team would test it carefully in a pilot.

3. A hospital asks for help reducing emergency waiting times. Name the five project phases and one concrete activity in each.

Show the answer

Scoping: agree the target, for example the share of patients seen within four hours, and the timeline. Hypotheses: guess that delays come from bed availability rather than triage. Analysis: map patient flow using timestamps and interview nurses and doctors on shift. Synthesis: show that most delay occurs while admitted patients wait for a ward bed, and recommend earlier discharge planning. Implementation: pilot the change on two wards and track waiting times weekly.

Where to go next

Read what a consultant does all day to see the work from the inside, then how case interviews work to see how firms test for it. When you are ready to try a full case, pick one from the casebook.
